Jean Bach’s passion for jazz has reaped an unexpected benefit for all jazz lovers. As a young woman she followed the Ellington band and became an expert on his music. Her first husband added his love of Basie and together they became amateur jazz historians. Jean gained media experience as producer of “The Arlene Francis Radio Show” and later with her involvement in “The Sound of Jazz” Television series. The famous Esquire jazz photo of 1959 gave her further opportunity to use her extensive knowledge and connections in the jazz world. She produced the documentary “A Great Day in Harlem,” which has been nominated for an Oscar, and brought about a renewed interest in the jazz personalities from that era. Life Magazine has re-staged the photo with the eleven remaining members and created a new montage of current jazz stars.
Jean was interviewed by Monk Rowe in New York City on October 18, 1995.

Good afternoon. We’re filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive, and we have a very interesting guest with us, Ms. Jean Bach. Welcome. This is special because we’ve had some musicians, we’ve had musicians’ wives and we’ve had an agent or two, but you’re the first film producer and “jazz source” I’m going to call you.

Well that’s true, I am in the film business now. But I used to be identified as a fan, and I felt well that’s rather important in the equation, you know you need fans. I was profiled in the New Yorker magazine in, about a dozen years ago. And the headline was “Fan.” And I thought well that’s pretty accurate.
It’s nice to know a lot about the music — when you get into filming it makes a big difference.
Yeah, well that’s actually how I was able to pull the film together more or less, because I had known the people involved for some years.

We should preface that we’re going to be talking about “A Great Day In Harlem,” which I know most of our viewers will know about already. But I’d like to ask you first how did you become such a fan of jazz music?
